resident.chief_complaint: Progressive motor weakness and tingling sensation in both upper and lower extremities.
resident.history: Motor weakness initially manifested ten months prior and started in the lower extremities before involving the upper extremities. The patient also developed tingling sensation and numbness in both upper and lower extremities. Three months after symptom onset, she was evaluated at the neurosurgery department of another university for progressive motor weakness and tingling sensation. She was able to walk independently but with an observable mild wide-base gait. She reported weight loss of 10 kg during 2 months. CT and MRI showed OPLL at the level of C3-T1 and cervical spinal cord compression; on T2-weighted images, high signal intensity was seen in the cervical spinal cord at the C5-6 disc space level. Electrophysiological tests (NCS/EMG) were not performed at that time.
resident.physical_exam: Physical examination revealed mild motor weakness (Medical Research Council [MRC] grade 4+/5) in all extremities and mildly decreased tactile sensation in all extremities. Gait was independently ambulatory with an observable mild wide-base pattern. Reflex findings are not documented.
key_positive_signs: Mild motor weakness (MRC 4+/5) in all extremities
Mildly decreased tactile sensation in all extremities
Weight loss of 10 kg over 2 months
OPLL at C3-T1 with cervical spinal cord compression on CT/MRI
High T2 signal intensity in cervical spinal cord at C5-6 disc space level

resident.public_message: This patient presents with a ten-month history of progressive motor weakness that began in the lower extremities and progressed to involve the upper extremities, along with tingling and numbness in all four limbs. She reports a 10 kg weight loss over 2 months. Examination shows mild motor weakness (MRC 4+/5) and mildly decreased tactile sensation in all extremities, with a mild wide-based gait. CT and MRI demonstrate OPLL from C3 to T1 with cervical spinal cord compression and T2 hyperintensity at C5-6. Electrophysiological testing was not performed. Past medical history is not documented.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record's description only; the films were not available for review. CT and MRI reportedly showed OPLL from C3-T1 with cervical spinal cord compression. The record does not specify compression direction or stenosis grade. T2-weighted imaging reportedly showed high signal intensity in the cervical cord at C5-6. These reported findings correlate highly with the described progressive myelopathic symptoms.

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord lesion (myelopathy), likely at C5-6 or multilevel due to C3-T1 OPLL. The pattern of progressive quadriparesis with sensory loss in all limbs and wide-based gait supports a cervical cord lesion, although upper motor neuron signs are not documented, so localization rests on an incomplete examination.

red_flags.finding: Weight loss of 10 kg over 2 months
red_flags.rationale: Unexplained by cervical cord compression; may indicate a systemic process (e.g., malignancy, metabolic) and warrants workup, but does not by itself provide an alternative explanation for the quadriparesis and sensory loss because the cord compression remains a plausible cause.
Absence of upper motor neuron signs (e.g., hyperreflexia, Babinski) prevents confirmation of myelopathy; this limits localization confidence but does not change the indication or plan.

Cannot exclude a coexisting peripheral neuropathy, which could contribute to symmetric weakness and sensory loss; this does not change current localization but should be considered if symptoms are atypical.

neurology.public_message: Localization is consistent with cervical myelopathy from C3-T1 OPLL, with T2 cord signal at C5-6. The clinical pattern—progressive quadriparesis with sensory loss in all limbs and wide-based gait—supports a cervical cord lesion, although upper motor neuron signs are not documented. Imaging-reported cord compression explains the dominant syndrome but not every finding. Red flags: (1) weight loss of 10 kg over 2 months—coexisting, unexplained by the cervical lesion and warrants systemic workup but does not currently offer an alternative cause; (2) reflex findings not documented—coexisting, limits confidence in myelopathic localization; (3) NCS/EMG not performed—coexisting, cannot exclude a peripheral neuropathy.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade II. Intraoperative MAP target 70 mmHg. Expected blood loss risk: moderate. Prone position tolerance: moderate. Extubation difficulty: unassessable because no airway assessment is documented. The record does not confirm systemic comorbidities; the 10 kg weight loss is unconfirmed and not used for grading.

preconditions_for_failure: Progressive worsening of motor strength or gait despite 3-6 months of structured conservative treatment
Development of new bowel or bladder dysfunction
Emergence of definitive upper motor neuron signs (e.g., hyperreflexia, spasticity, Babinski)
Radiographic progression of cord compression or T2 signal change on follow-up MRI
physiatrist_opening.public_message: This patient has mild myelopathy (MRC 4+/5, independent ambulation) from C3-T1 OPLL with T2 cord signal at C5-6. While progressive symptoms over 10 months and T2 signal change raise concern and argue against indefinite delay, a structured 3-6 month trial of conservative management remains a rational first step in the absence of clear upper motor neuron signs or rapid deterioration. Conservative care—including physical therapy, gait and balance training, posture modification, pain management, and close neurologic monitoring—has a reported success rate of about 50% for mild myelopathy, though outcomes are less predictable when cord signal change is present. I cannot overstate success beyond that. I strongly recommend completing the missing reflex examination and NCS/EMG before deciding surgery; weight loss also warrants systemic workup but does not preclude a conservative trial. Failure of conservative treatment should be declared only if any of my listed preconditions occur.

vice_opinions.assessment: The patient presents with a 10-month history of progressive myelopathic symptoms, mild weakness, and sensory changes, with imaging showing OPLL from C3 to T1 causing cord compression and T2 hyperintensity at C5-6. The T2 signal change indicates likely intramedullary damage and increases concern for further neurological deterioration if compression is not relieved. However, several essential elements are missing: upper motor neuron signs are not documented, NCS/EMG have not been performed, and the 10 kg weight loss remains unexplained. These gaps create uncertainty about the completeness of the myelopathic syndrome and about possible systemic disease that might affect surgical risk or prognosis. From a spine surgery standpoint, surgical decompression is a defensible option given the progressive course and cord signal change, but a period of diagnostic clarification and possibly conservative management could also be defended. I do not have a firm preference between these paths without more information.
proposed_options: Proceed with surgical decompression now (posterior cervical laminectomy and fusion or anterior decompression/fusion depending on OPLL morphology) to halt progression, accepting the incomplete medical workup.

First complete the missing diagnostic elements—full neurologic examination with reflexes, NCS/EMG, and systemic evaluation for weight loss—then reassess for surgery, with surgery if no contraindication and myelopathy confirmed.

Begin a structured conservative management program with close neurologic monitoring (e.g., every 2–4 weeks), proceed to surgery if any deterioration or failure to improve, while completing the workup in parallel.
disagreement_points: The physiatrist recommends a 3–6 month conservative trial, but the progressive nature and T2 cord signal argue that delay may increase the risk of irreversible deficit; I would ask whether a shorter monitoring interval or earlier surgery threshold would be safer.

The absence of documented upper motor neuron signs and the unexplained 10 kg weight loss are unusual for straightforward OPLL myelopathy and could indicate a coexisting peripheral or systemic process; I would not want to commit to surgery without at least addressing these, but I defer to your risk tolerance.
deferred_questions_to_director: Would you prefer to proceed with surgical decompression now, given the progressive myelopathy and T2 signal, or should we first complete the reflex examination, NCS/EMG, and systemic workup for the weight loss?
If a conservative trial is chosen, what monitoring interval and failure criteria would you set given the documented progression and cord signal change?
If surgery is planned, what approach would you favor for C3-T1 OPLL (anterior versus posterior) and should we obtain additional imaging such as flexion/extension films or CT myelogram?

If workup identifies an alternative cause or significantly alters risk, conservative management will be pursued; otherwise, surgical decompression will be planned.
